title: Turing Machines and Computability
tagline: The Turing machine defines what computation means — and the halting problem proves there are questions no algorithm can ever answer.

sections.content:
A **Turing machine (TM)** is an idealised computer: a finite control unit attached to an infinite tape divided into cells, each holding a symbol from a finite alphabet. A read/write head can move left or right one cell at a time. At each step the machine reads the current cell, writes a symbol, moves the head, and transitions to a new state — all according to a finite transition table.

Despite its simplicity, the Turing machine can simulate **any algorithm** — this is the **Church-Turing thesis**, the foundational claim that the informal notion of 'algorithm' equals the formal notion of Turing-computable function. The thesis cannot be proved (it equates a mathematical object with an informal concept), but no counterexample has ever been found. Its dark corollary is that **some problems are uncomputable**: no TM can solve them, regardless of resources.

flowchart LR
    A["Tape: ... a a b b ..."] --> B["Read/Write Head"]
    B --> C["Finite Control"]
    C --> D["Transition Function\nδ(state, symbol)\n= (new_state, write, L/R)"]
    D --> B
    C --> E["Accept"]
    C --> F["Reject"]
sections.caption: Turing machine anatomy. The finite control (the 'brain') has finitely many states; the tape provides unlimited memory. On each step: read symbol, write symbol, move head left or right, change state.

sections.title: An Infinite Notepad with a Cursor
sections.content:
Think of the TM tape as an **infinite notepad** and the head as a cursor you can move left or right. You have a rulebook (the transition table): 'if the page under the cursor says X and you are in mood Y, write Z, move right, switch to mood W'. Your 'mood' is the finite state. The notepad is unlimited, so you can jot down arbitrarily complex intermediate results — unlike the finite automaton (no notepad) or the PDA (only a stack, not a 2D page).

The **halting problem** is asking: 'given any rulebook and any initial notepad, does the person eventually stop?' You might think you can check by watching them, but the trouble is they might keep going *forever* — and you never know if they're about to stop or will run for another trillion steps. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no rulebook (program) can answer this question for all possible inputs.

A **Turing machine** is a 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject) where Q is the state set, Σ the input alphabet, Γ ⊇ Σ the tape alphabet (including a blank symbol ␣), δ: Q×Γ → Q×Γ×{L,R} the transition function, q₀ the start state, and q_accept, q_reject the halting states. A TM *accepts* its input if it halts in q_accept; it *rejects* if it halts in q_reject; it may also *loop forever*.

The **halting problem**: given a TM description ⟨M⟩ and input w, does M halt on w? Turing proved this is **undecidable** using a diagonal argument. Suppose decider H exists. Build TM D that on input ⟨M⟩: runs H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and does the opposite (loop if H says halt, halt if H says loop). Run D on ⟨D⟩ — contradiction in both cases. Therefore H cannot exist.

**Decidable vs. recognisable**: a language is *decidable* (recursive) if some TM always halts and correctly accepts/rejects. It is *Turing-recognisable* (recursively enumerable, RE) if some TM halts and accepts for strings in the language, but may loop on strings not in the language. The halting problem is RE but not decidable. Its complement (TMs that do NOT halt) is not even RE — it is co-RE. This hierarchy — decidable ⊂ RE, with undecidable languages outside — is the foundation of computability theory.

flowchart TD
    A["All Decision Problems"] --> B["Undecidable\n(no TM halts on all inputs)"]
    B --> C["Turing-Recognisable (RE)\n(TM halts on YES inputs)"]
    C --> D["Decidable (Recursive)\n(TM always halts)"]
    D --> E["Context-Sensitive"]

    F --> G["Regular"]
sections.caption: Computability hierarchy. Decidable problems sit inside the larger RE class; undecidable problems (like the halting problem) are RE but not decidable. Below decidable: the Chomsky grammar hierarchy.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The `{aⁿbⁿcⁿ}` recogniser shows TM power: a CFG/PDA can match two counts but not three simultaneously. The halting problem pseudo-proof is the diagonal argument: a hypothetical halter is used to build a program that contradicts its own output. Rice's theorem — a far-reaching generalisation — makes it clear that any meaningful question about program behaviour is undecidable.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Practical takeaway from undecidability:** linters, type checkers, and static analysers are *sound-but-incomplete* (they may flag false positives) or *complete-but-unsound* (they may miss real bugs) — never both perfect and general. Rice's theorem guarantees no tool can detect all bugs and nothing else. This is why security tools, compilers, and formal verifiers report 'conservative approximations' rather than exact answers.

items: A **Turing machine** has a finite control (states) and an infinite tape (memory); it can simulate any algorithm — the most powerful model of computation we know.
The **Church-Turing thesis**: all reasonable models of computation (lambda calculus, RAM machines, programming languages) compute the same class of functions as Turing machines.
The **halting problem** — does TM M halt on input w? — is undecidable: no TM can answer it correctly for all (M, w) pairs. Proved by Turing's diagonal argument in 1936.
**Decidable** languages have TMs that always halt; **Turing-recognisable (RE)** languages have TMs that halt on YES instances but may loop on NO instances.
**Rice's theorem**: any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable — the fundamental limit of static analysis and program verification.

quiz.question: What does the Church-Turing thesis claim?
options: Turing machines are the fastest model of computation.
Every effectively computable function is computable by a Turing machine.
All programming languages are equivalent to finite automata.
The halting problem can be solved by a sufficiently powerful computer.
quiz.explanation: The Church-Turing thesis equates the informal notion of 'algorithm' with the formal notion of Turing computability. It cannot be proved mathematically (it relates a formal object to an informal concept) but is universally accepted based on evidence.

quiz.question: What is the halting problem?
options: The problem of finding the minimum number of states in a DFA.
Deciding whether a given Turing machine halts on a given input.
Deciding whether a context-free grammar is ambiguous.
Determining the running time of a program.
quiz.explanation: The halting problem asks: given a TM M and input w, does M eventually halt? Turing proved in 1936 that no TM can correctly answer this for all (M, w) pairs — it is undecidable.

quiz.question: Turing's proof that the halting problem is undecidable relies on:
options: Proof by induction on the number of states.
A diagonalisation argument: assuming a halter exists and deriving a contradiction.
Reduction from the satisfiability problem.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems directly.
quiz.explanation: Turing constructed a machine D that, given any machine M, does the opposite of what a hypothetical halter H predicts for M on input ⟨M⟩. Running D on ⟨D⟩ produces a contradiction — so H cannot exist.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a Turing-decidable and a Turing-recognisable language?
options: Decidable languages are finite; recognisable languages are infinite.
Decidable TMs always halt; recognisable TMs may loop on strings NOT in the language.
Recognisable languages are a subset of decidable languages.
Decidable languages require exponential time; recognisable languages run in polynomial time.
quiz.explanation: A decidable (recursive) language has a TM that always halts with ACCEPT or REJECT. A recognisable (RE) language has a TM that halts and accepts strings in the language, but may loop forever on strings not in the language — you never get a definitive REJECT.

quiz.question: What does Rice's theorem state?
options: Every computable function can be computed in polynomial time.
Every non-trivial semantic property of Turing machines is undecidable.
Context-free languages are a subset of decidable languages.
The halting problem is solvable for finite programs.
quiz.explanation: Rice's theorem says: if P is any property of the language of a TM (not just its mechanics), and P is non-trivial (some TMs have it, some don't), then deciding P is undecidable. This kills hopes of a perfect general-purpose program analyser.

quiz.question: The language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0} is recognisable by a Turing machine but not by a pushdown automaton. Why?
options: A PDA cannot read the symbol 'c'.
A PDA has only one stack and cannot simultaneously count three equal quantities; a TM can use its tape as arbitrary memory.
Context-free languages are not closed under concatenation.
A TM is always faster than a PDA, so it handles more languages.
quiz.explanation: A PDA's single stack can match one pair of counts (e.g. a's with b's), but not both a=b and b=c simultaneously. A TM can mark symbols on its tape in multiple passes, counting all three independently.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of an undecidable problem?
options: Deciding if a string matches a regular expression.
Deciding if a context-free grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form.
Deciding if two arbitrary programs always produce the same output (program equivalence).
Deciding if a DFA accepts the empty string.
quiz.explanation: Program equivalence is undecidable by reduction from the halting problem (a consequence of Rice's theorem). The other problems — regex matching, CNF check, and DFA empty-string acceptance — are all decidable.

quiz.question: Which of the following models of computation is NOT Turing-equivalent?
options: Lambda calculus
JavaScript (with unbounded memory)
Pushdown automaton
Random-access machine (RAM)
quiz.explanation: A pushdown automaton is equivalent to CFGs — less powerful than a Turing machine. Lambda calculus, RAM machines, and programming languages like JavaScript (given unbounded memory) are all Turing-equivalent.

quiz.question: Why can't a program perfectly detect all security vulnerabilities in arbitrary code?
options: Security properties are too complex to represent as a grammar.
Rice's theorem: any non-trivial property of program behaviour is undecidable.
Cryptographic algorithms prevent static analysis.
Security requires running code dynamically, which is exponential.
quiz.explanation: Rice's theorem implies that any non-trivial semantic property — including 'does this program have a vulnerability?' — is undecidable. Static analysers must therefore be approximations: they have false positives, false negatives, or both.

quiz.question: What are the two components of a Turing machine that together give it unlimited memory?
options: A finite state set and an infinite stack.
A finite transition function and an infinite tape.
An infinite state set and a finite alphabet.
A finite control and multiple finite tapes.
quiz.explanation: A TM has a *finite* transition function (the 'program') and an *infinite* tape (the 'memory'). The finiteness of the control is what distinguishes it from 'just any computer with infinite RAM'; the tape is what gives it power beyond finite automata and PDAs.
